abstract: I develop a theory of state-dependent signal extraction in price setting. Firms infer how much sectoral price movements reflect persistent aggregate or transitory sector-specific disturbances. When inflation is low relative to sectoral variation, sticky-price firms discount competitor movements because following transitory movements risks leaving them mispriced. As inflation rises relative to sectoral noise, firms increasingly attribute these movements to aggregate shocks and sticky firms respond more strongly. UK micro-price data support these predictions: below approximately 1.9% sectoral inflation, sticky firms respond less to competitors than flexible firms; above it, the gap closes. This convergence generates state-dependent aggregate inflation dynamics.
title: A Signal-Extraction Theory of Inflation Pass-Through

abstract: We analyze firms’ perceptions of their cost of capital using hand-collected data. The perceived cost of capital is associated with the allocation of capital across firms. In a model with inefficient financial markets, firms can maximize their current market value by setting their perceived cost of capital equal to the expected returns on their debt and equity. In the data, little variation in firms’ perceived cost of capital can be justified by variation in expected returns, suggesting that firms do not follow this market-value maximization benchmark. Alternatively, firms may aim to maximize their “fair value” corrected for financial market inefficiencies. In the data, a fair-value benchmark (based on the CAPM) can justify half the variation in the perceived cost of capital. However, most of the variation can be justified by the beliefs of financial analysts about expected returns. Using a quantitative model, we find that the observed distortions in the perceived cost of capital can substantially impact capital allocation and thereby reduce aggregate productivity.
title: Firms’ Perceived Cost of Capital

abstract: Can tourism-oriented place-based policies stimulate corporate green innovation? Using 21,921 firm-year observations of Chinese A-share listed firms across 240 prefecture-level cities from 2003 to 2024, this study exploits the staggered designation of China’s 5 A National Tourist Attractions as a quasi-natural experiment. Staggered difference-in-differences estimates show that 5 A designation significantly increases corporate green patenting. Further analyses reveal three complementary pathways: designation heightens local government environmental attention, strengthens public environmental attention, and enhances firms’ environmental orientation, all of which are positively associated with corporate green innovation. Subsample analyses reveal variation in the estimated innovation response across firms with different tourism relevance, absorptive capacity, and pollution characteristics. Spatial analyses further indicate that the innovation response extends beyond designated cities through cross-city linkages. These findings demonstrate that tourism quality certification can reshape firms’ environmental innovation incentives beyond its primary tourism objective, broadening the policy foundations of green technological change and highlighting the environmental innovation consequences of place-based development policies.

abstract: Although electric vehicles (EVs) are a climate-friendly alternative to internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEVs), EV adoption is challenged by higher up-front procurement prices. Existing discourse attributes this price differential to high battery costs and assumes that lowering these costs to below $100/kWh will create upfront cost parity between EVs and ICEVs. Does existing data support such reasoning? What factors beyond battery cost impact EV prices? And what relative influence do battery and non-battery factors have on price? Leveraging data for over 400 EV models and trims sold in the United States (US) between 2011 and 2023, we address these questions. We find that, counterintuitively, the average manufacturer's suggested retail price (MSRP) of EVs has increased over time despite declining EV battery costs. During the same period, we observe substantial increases in horsepower and the number of vehicle features, both of which are significant predictors of rising EV prices. Moreover, our analyses suggest that future reductions in pack-level battery costs are unlikely to deliver price parity between EVs and ICEVs. We estimate that were battery packs to cost $100/kWh, a threshold considered pivotal to achieving ICEV-EV price parity and motivating widespread EV affordability, average EV prices would decline by just $5088. These findings warrant attention as decarbonization efforts increasingly emphasize EVs as a pathway for complying with domestic and international climate agreements.
title: Enumerating predictors of electric vehicle prices

abstract: This study examines how strengthening creditor rights can have unintended capital-market consequences by reshaping investors' perceptions of firms whose controlling shareholders (promoters) pledge shares. Exploiting India's Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), enacted in 2016, as a quasi-natural experiment, we find no significant pre-reform association between pledging and crash risk, consistent with the signaling benefits and agency costs of pledging offsetting each other. Following IBC implementation, however, pledging firms experienced significantly higher crash risk, consistent with heightened creditor enforcement increasing the risk of promoter control loss. This increase is more pronounced in regions with higher district judicial capacity, providing further evidence consistent with the enforcement mechanism. Channel analysis supports the ownership-loss mechanism, although the evidence from ownership-based subsample tests is mixed. Turnover interactions further suggest that investor disagreement amplifies the post-IBC increase in crash risk among pledging firms experiencing deteriorating promoter ownership. The increase is also more pronounced among firms with excessive pledging but weaker among dividend-paying firms. Overall, our findings show that stronger creditor rights make promoter control fragility more consequential, increasing investor disagreement and crash risk, highlighting the unintended capital-market consequences of reforms designed to strengthen creditor protection.
title: Strengthening pledgee rights and stock price crash risk

abstract: Long viewed as a flexible and tax-efficient way to return cash to shareholders, share repurchases have recently come under growing public criticism, triggering political and regulatory responses. We find that public sentiment, as reflected in negative media coverage of share repurchases, deters share repurchase activity. Political risk is an important channel for this relation, as politically sensitive firms exhibit a greater reduction in repurchase activity in response to negative public sentiment. When we analyze the consequences of sentiment-induced share repurchase reductions, we find that the reduced repurchases exacerbate, rather than mitigate, agency problems. Instead of switching to dividends, firms reduce overall payout, hold excess cash at a discounted market valuation, and pursue inefficient investments, all of which suggests diminished shareholder welfare. Taken together, our evidence shows that in a political economy skeptical of corporations, public sentiment can influence corporate payout policies, even at the expense of shareholder interests.
title: Public Sentiment and Share Repurchases

abstract: This paper investigates trading mechanisms for efficiently (re)allocating a good to agents who face liquidity constraints and have private information about their valuation. I derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of ex post efficient, interim incentive compatible, interim individually rational, ex post budget balanced and ex post liquidity constrained trading mechanisms. Applying the framework to partnership dissolution problems, I show that efficient buyouts are more likely when initial ownership shares are tilted toward less liquid partners and away from more financially flexible ones. For practical implementation, I propose an auction format that implements the liquidity-constrained mechanism in a simple and operational way. Finally, I demonstrate that increasing the number of participants raises the liquidity resources required to sustain efficient trade, suggesting that larger markets may exacerbate financial frictions rather than alleviate them.
title: Asymmetric Information, Liquidity Constraints, and Efficient Trade

abstract: This paper provides identification results for the causal effect of treatment on binary outcomes, considering both ordered (nesting binary treatments as a special case) and continuous treatments. Within a quantile regression framework, treatment endogeneity is characterized by the joint distribution (copula) of unobserved errors. Identification is achieved using instrumental variables and a shape restriction on the copula.
title: Identification of the causal effect of treatment on binary outcomes

abstract: Two formats are commonly used to report grouped income data. The first provides group population shares and income bounds which can be represented as a histogram. The second presents group population shares with income shares (or mean incomes) which can be represented as a (generalised) Lorenz curve. The purpose of this paper is to compare the two formats. We show that the Lorenz curve format tends to produce more efficient but less robust estimators of distributional parameters and of inequality measures. JEL Codes C13, C16, D31
title: Histogram vs Lorenz

abstract: This paper investigates the role of outward multinational enterprise (MNE) networks in shaping regional resilience to financial stress episodes, using regional, sectoral, and firm-level data for the entire sample of NUTS-2 EU regions. The results suggest that regions and sectors with a greater presence of outward-oriented MNE groups—comprising locally headquartered parent firms and their foreign subsidiaries—experience significantly smaller output declines following domestic stress. A Rajan-Zingales-style analysis further shows that sectors characterized by higher external financial dependence are more adversely affected, but this vulnerability is substantially attenuated in regions with larger outward MNE networks. The findings are consistent with the view that MNE networks enhance regional resilience by facilitating access to internal capital markets and cross-border funding when domestic credit conditions deteriorate.
title: Multinational enterprise networks and regional resilience to financial shocks

abstract: Understanding technology adoption processes is crucial for agricultural policy and research, yet most studies rely on mean-based models that may obscure distributional differences. This study investigates precision agriculture technology adoption intensity using survey data collected between December 2024 and January 2025 from 342 German farmers. Adoption intensity is measured as the number of technologies used from a portfolio of 32 technologies and analysed by quantile count regression alongside negative binomial regression. Results reveal that risk attitude shows stable associations with across all quantiles, while farm succession exhibits increasing associations. Results demonstrate limitations of mean-based approaches and provide insights for stakeholders.
title: A quantile count regression analysis of precision agriculture technology adoption intensity

abstract: International climate commitments depend on sustained commitments, yet the United States policy reversals reveal that participation is a recurring political choice rather than a one-time decision. We develop a two-region stochastic integrated assessment model in which US compliance with Paris Agreement aligned emissions caps follows a Markov-switching process, then solve its associated feedback Nash equilibria with state-contingent mitigation and consumption strategies. Our results show that the US climate policy uncertainty generates substantial dispersion in emissions and abatement costs. Moreover, welfare effects are asymmetric: US gains from intermittent free-riding (mean consumption-equivalent variation of $455 per capita per year) while the rest of the world (RoW) incurs losses ($43 per capita per year) driven primarily by higher expected climate damages, with a global aggregate loss of $149 billion per year. Furthermore, when policy uncertainty instead arises in RoW, global effects are muted because their emissions cap remains slack during much of the transition, so spillovers operate mainly through damages rather than strategic mitigation.
journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
source_issue: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
title: Strategic spillovers of time inconsistency risk in climate commitment

abstract: We propose a cultural transmission model based on the co-evolution of cultural traits, behaviors, and socialization levels. Cultural traits affect agents’ behavior during their interaction in a strategic environment. In turn, behaviors affect how much parents directly socialize their children. The co-evolution of cultural traits and behaviors across two cultural groups microfounds well-established acculturation processes: assimilation, integration, marginalization, and separation. We characterize how the occurrence of each process depends on the nature of the strategic environment (complements or substitutes), on whether material payoffs vary across interactions within a period or remain fixed, and on the costs of transmitting a trait.
title: An Economic Model of Acculturation under Strategic Complements and Substitutes

abstract: What are the macroeconomic and distributional effects of large cash transfers when implemented at scale? We develop a two-region, small open economy heterogeneous-agent model with occupational choice, financial and real frictions, and labor mobility across regions. We discipline the model with baseline data from a new large-scale experiment in rural Malawi. In the model, transfers generate a sharp increase in consumption and a more persistent expansion in productive expenditures, especially intermediate inputs. There is substantial heterogeneity within and across regions: lower-wealth households exhibit the largest consumption response, while wealthier entrepreneurs account for much of the expansion in capital and intermediate input use. Through labor-market spillovers, workers in non-treated regions benefit, whereas entrepreneurs there are adversely affected. These effects gradually dissipate as the economy converges back to its pre-transfer equilibrium.
title: Predicting the effects of a large-scale cash transfer: Financial frictions, occupational choice, and local labor markets

abstract: We examine how disclosure processing costs influence SEC monitoring of firm disclosures by leveraging the mandatory adoption of XBRL—a digital reporting language designed to reduce these costs. Post adoption, both the frequency and quality of SEC comment letters for 10-K filings increase. Additional tests suggest that XBRL enhances SEC monitoring through three channels. First, automated data extraction improves review efficiency, as reflected in more timely comment letters and greater XBRL benefits when the SEC faces tighter resource constraints or uses XBRL analytical tools. Second, standardized reporting strengthens the SEC’s benchmarking ability: firms using more standardized tags and tags more comparable to those of industry peers benefit more. Third, XBRL facilitates SEC scrutiny of complex reporting issues, yielding more frequent and higher-quality comments on noncore earnings accounts and for firms with more footnote tags or complex filings. Overall, our evidence suggests that reduced disclosure processing costs enhance the SEC’s regulatory monitoring.
title: XBRL adoption and SEC monitoring

abstract: This study examines how minimum wage increases affect the mental health of low-wage workers in China. We leverage temporal and county-level variation in minimum wage adjustments from 2010 to 2020 to estimate their causal effects. To identify individuals most likely affected by minimum wage increases, we adopt two complementary strategies: one based on historical wage distributions and another using a demographics-based machine learning approach. We find that minimum wage increases significantly reduce depression among affected workers, whereas no discernible effect is observed for a placebo group of workers less likely to be exposed to the policy. The mental health benefits are especially pronounced among individuals more susceptible to mental illness. Mechanism analyses indicate that these improvements are driven primarily by higher income, increased consumption, and reinforced economic security. By documenting the mental health benefits of minimum wage increases, our research highlights the role of such policies in promoting subjective well-being.

abstract: Physicists could already explain the motion of planets with extraordinary precision centuries ago. Finance still struggles to explain yesterday’s stock market movement. This column identifies a foundational failure of empirical asset pricing and makes significant progress towards explaining market movements using AI. Conventional measures account for remarkably little return variation, even with hindsight. Reasons extracted with AI from just one Wall Street Journal market recap per trading day explain about 30% of daily and 40% of monthly S&P 500 return variation out of sample.
authors: Bryan Kelly, Yinan Su, Chao Zhang
title: Explaining the stock market: Why is it still so hard?

abstract: Advanced economies are counting on artificial intelligence to revive productivity growth just as their workforces age. This column argues that the two trends are closely connected, because young workers adopt new technologies at far higher rates than old workers. Evidence from US local labour markets shows that younger workforces adopt more technology, see faster wage growth, and generate more innovation. A model calibrated to these responses attributes about one quarter of the late-1990s US productivity boom to the baby boom’s youth wave. Workforce ageing is thus a headwind to adoption-driven growth, though it need not diminish the gains from an AI-scale breakthrough.
title: The demographics of technology adoption and productivity growth

abstract: Governments use tax incentives to encourage innovation, but their benefits may extend beyond the firms claiming them. Using the Dutch innovation box and linked employer-employee data, this column shows that firms share part of their additional after-tax profits with incumbent workers, including those not directly engaged in R&D. Higher wages also coincide with lower job-to-job mobility among non-R&D workers. These findings highlight the labour market consequences of innovation policy.
title: Rent sharing under innovation tax breaks

abstract: This study examines the nonlinear relationship between cross-border data flow restrictions and firm resilience using panel data on Chinese A-share manufacturing firms from 2014 to 2022. We find an inverted U-shaped relationship: moderate restrictions enhance resilience by strengthening data security and supply chain efficiency, whereas excessive restrictions weaken resilience by increasing compliance costs and technological rigidity. Digital transformation significantly moderates this relationship by flattening the inverted U-shaped curve. Greater digital transformation attenuates both the resilience-enhancing effect of low-intensity restrictions and the resilience-reducing effect of high-intensity restrictions, reducing firms’ sensitivity to regulatory intensity. Heterogeneity analysis shows that these effects are stronger among firms in eastern regions, technology-intensive firms, and firms with lower supply chain transparency. The findings demonstrate that the resilience effects of cross-border data regulation depend critically on regulatory intensity and firms’ digital capabilities. The results highlight the importance of differentiated policies that balance data security, cross-border data use, and firms’ adaptability within global value chains.

abstract: This paper extends the sustainable-consumption benchmark of Campbell and Martin (2025) to an Epstein–Zin recursive-utility setting. The purpose is not to replace the Campbell–Martin certainty-equivalent mechanism, but to separate two preference channels that are mechanically tied together under time-separable CRRA utility. Risk aversion determines the optimal portfolio and the certainty-equivalent return r CE , and hence the risk-sensitive ceiling in β ⋆ = min { β , r CE } . Conditional on β ⋆ and r CE , the elasticity of intertemporal substitution parameterizes the affine mapping into the sustainable consumption–wealth ratio. Sustainability is formulated as a conditional non-declining requirement on the recursive continuation-welfare process. Thus the criterion is imposed on recursive certainty-equivalent welfare rather than on a time-additive utility sum. Using the conditional non-declining welfare formulation and the sustainable-HJB verification principle for submartingale performance processes, we obtain a closed-form characterization in the Brownian benchmark. The sustainable consumption–wealth ratio is the smaller of the unconstrained Epstein–Zin consumption–wealth ratio and the certainty-equivalent return generated by the Merton portfolio. The risky share remains the Merton share. The contribution is a recursive decomposition into an asset-pricing and discount-rate-ceiling channel, operating through risk aversion, the Merton portfolio, and r CE , and an intertemporal-substitution channel, through which ψ maps ( β ⋆ , r CE ) into the sustainable consumption–wealth ratio.
title: Recursive utility, social discounting, and sustainable consumption
